title: Socialism USA 2.0
author: David Rosen
content:

Photograph Source: Morgan.rice.bassline.design - [CC BY

The U.S. is witnessing a revival of “socialism.” A century ago, during the
1910s-1920s, more than 1,000 socialists were
[elected](https://depts.washington.edu/moves/SP_map-elected.shtml) to public
office, including two members of Congress, dozens of state legislators and
more than 130 mayors.

Today, there are three “democratic socialists” in Congress – Sen. Bernie
Sanders (I-VT) and two in the House, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) and
Rashida Tlaib (D-MI). Zohran Mamdani brought a spotlight to this development
when he was elected mayor in New York City in 2025; other socialist mayors
include Katie Wilson (Seattle) and Emma Mulvaney-Stanak (Montpelier, VT).

[_Rolling Stone_](https://www.rollingstone.com/politics/politics-
features/democratic-socialists-zohran-mamdani-win-1235408412) and
[Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Democratic_Socialists_of_America_public_officeholders)
claim there are 250 elected officials affiliated with the Democratic Socialist
of America (DSA). Still other groups – e.g., Working Families Party (WFP) and
Green Party – are socialist all but in name.

According to the [ _Washington
Examine_](https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/news/campaigns/congressional/4624938/over-30-socialists-
won-primaries-2026-elections/) _r_ , candidates endorsed by the DSA scored
victories in 35 primary elections so far in 2026 including – in its words –
“upsets against entrenched incumbents.” Going further, it notes: “The DSA has
backed 150 candidates this cycle: 35 advanced from their primaries or were
unopposed, while 34 have lost. Some of the wins include incumbents in federal
or local government.”

Among these candidates are:

\+ Christopher Rabb -- re-elected to Pennsylvania House of Representatives
District 200 in November 2024.

\+ Claire Valdez -- won in New York’s 7th Congressional District.

\+ Darializa Avila Chevalier -- unseated Rep. Adriano Espaillat in New York’s
13th District.

\+ Brad Lander -- beat incumbent Dan Goldman in the 10th District.

\+ [Abdul El-Sayed](https://www.newyorker.com/news/the-new-yorker-
interview/abdul-el-sayeds-argument-for-america-and-against-his-own-party) –
won the Democratic nomination for Senate in Michigan.

\+ Melat Kiros – defeated U.S. Rep. Diana DeGette in Colorado’s 1st
Congressional District.

\+ Adam Bojak -- won a three-way Democratic primary for the New York State
Assembly in the Buffalo area.

\+ Maurice “Mo” Brown -- [narrowly
defeated](https://centralcurrent.org/maurice-mo-brown-declares-victory-while-
magnarelli-concedes-in-democratic-primary-for-assembly-seat/) Assemblyman
William B. Magnarelli New York's 129th state Assembly District.

\+ [Donavan
McKinney](https://ballotpedia.org/Donavan_McKinney#google_vignette) – Michigan
state representative (11th House District) is running for Congress.

\+ [Janeese Lewis George](https://www.theguardian.com/us-
news/2026/jun/28/democratic-socialist-mayor-mamdani-wilson) -- is expected to
win the mayoral race in Washington, DC.

\+ Nithya Raman, a LA City Councilwomen – will challenge incumbent mayor Karen
Bass for mayor.

The most noted defeat of a socialist was that of Francesca Hong who lost to
David Crowley in the primary race for Wisconsin governor.

The rise of Socialism 2.0 in the U.S. speaks as much to the appeal of a more
“socially” conscious democracy as it does to the faltering, old-money
Democratic Party and Pres. Trump’s failures during his second term in office.

A September 2025 [Gallup poll](https://news.gallup.com/poll/694835/image-
capitalism-slips.aspx) found two-thirds of Democrats (66%) had a favorable
view of socialism while two-in-five (42%) had a “negative” image of it. Nearly
40 percent (38%) of “Independents” had a favorable view of socialism. Even
more revealing, last year the libertarian [Cato Institute
reported](https://www.cato.org/blog/young-americans-socialism-too-much-thats-
problem-libertarians-must-fix) 62 percent of Americans aged 18–29 say they
hold a “favorable view” of socialism.

Further insight into the growing appeal of socialism is reflected in an August
1026 poll conducted by [Navigator Research](https://www.cato.org/blog/young-
americans-socialism-too-much-thats-problem-libertarians-must-fix). It found:

\+ Socialist Democrats skew younger, with 57% of them being between the ages
of 18 and 44, while 48% of MAGA Republicans are aged 55 and up.

\+ A plurality of Socialist Democrats have white-collar jobs (36%), while a
plurality (34%) of MAGA Republicans have blue-collar jobs.

\+ Both groups are majority white, however MAGA Republicans more so (86% of
MAGA Republicans, 64% of Social Democrats). 26% and 17% of Socialist Democrats
are Black and Latino, respectively.

\+ A majority of MAGA Republicans are homeowners (55%), while a plurality of
Social Democrats rent their homes (48%).

Clarifying its findings, Navigator noted:

> _Self-identified democratic socialists do not see socialism as being
> mutually exclusive and continue to identify with other terms on the left,
> including more mainstream Democratic labels. Of Socialist Democrats, 92%
> consider themselves to also be Democrats, 84% consider themselves to also be
> Obama Democrats, and 80% consider themselves to also be progressive._

Giving voice to this development, [Ravi
Mangla](https://courthousenews.com/democratic-socialists-surge-in-mayoral-
races-across-the-country-as-anti-trump-fervor-rises/) of the WFP insists,
“It’s not folks looking for the leftmost option so much as looking for a
candidate who’s gonna be on their side.” Adding, “It’s less about whether you
are on the right or on the left so much as whether you are willing to punch up
at the powerful.”

NYC’s Mamdani and Washington’s Lewis George, among others, are self-described
“sewer socialists” who emphasize the need for responsive government services
rather than critiques of market economics. In New York City, the “Commie
Corridor” stretches through parts of the Northern Brooklyn to Western Queens
and refers to young, leftist and college-age voters. As reported by the [
_Gothamist,_](https://gothamist.com/news/a-peoples-guide-to-the-commie-
corridor-of-brooklyn-and-queens)

> _The highest concentration of card-carrying democratic socialists lives in
> these neighborhoods, where the winning candidates appealed to voters
> struggling to keep up with rising rents and angry at politicians in both
> parties who are sending their taxpayer money to conflicts abroad._

The tendency toward America’s “Socialism 2.0” is not limited to New York and
other radical progressives. On his [Substack
post](https://robertreich.substack.com/p/trumps-state-
socialism?r=o8wo7&utm_campaign=post&utm_medium=email&triedRedirect=true) on
June 15, 2026, the economist Robert Reich identified Pres. Trump’s economic
policies as “national socialism.” As he wrote, “Trump’s national socialism is
concentrating ever more power in Trump’s hands. A whole new range of decisions
is being made about the U.S. economy but without any congressional oversight
or public knowledge.” Reich stresses that the Trump 2.0 regime has escalated
federal investment in – and equity ownership of – traditionally private
corporations.

Most revealing, White House
[reports](https://www.whitehouse.gov/investments/;%20see%20also%20https:/www.nytimes.com/2025/11/25/us/politics/trump-
intel-steel-minerals-china.html;%20and%20https:/www.cato.org/commentary/uncle-
sam-shareholder) – in an undated post — that total “U.S. and Foreign
Investments” are $10.7 trillion to both independent countries (e.g., UAE,
Qatar, Saudi Arabia) and private companies (e.g., Apple, Amazon, AT&T and
many, many others). Arnab Datta, of Employ America, [points
out](https://www.employamerica.org/expanding-the-toolkit/a-users-guide-to-
government-equity-investing/), “Not since the Great Depression has the
government taken ownership stakes in private corporations at such scale and
speed, and in this case, without explicit Congressional authorization.”

In addition to the federal investments, a slew of other indicators suggests
the U.S.’s deepening “socialist” economy. These include the growing
federalization of health care; according to the Committee for Responsible
Federal Budget (CRFB), federal spending on [health
care](https://www.crfb.org/blogs/cbo-projects-high-federal-health-program-
costs) totaled $1.8 trillion in 2025 and is projected to grow 63% by 2036 to
$3.1 trillion. (Total [military spending](https://usafacts.org/answers/how-
much-does-the-us-spend-on-defense/country/united-states/) for 2025 is
estimated at $916 billion.)

Compounding these developments, the Trump-led reactionary government (often
with the passive support of establishment Democrats) has contributed to the
country’s increasing income and wealth inequality; the St. Louis Federal
Reserve [estimates](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/WFRBST01134) that the
top 1 percent of American households control roughly 32 percent of the
nation's total wealth. And the [richest 10
percent](https://inequality.org/facts/wealth-inequality/#household-wealth) of
American households now own over two-thirds of the nation’s total wealth.

The worst, long-term consequence of the Trump presidency will likely be the
ever-greater environmental crisis that defines the global natural order.
Climate change is getting worse every day and (almost) everyone is – or will
be – suffering from it. Sadly, Trump and his super-rich billionaire “bros”
will find ways to ignore or hide from this truth.

The current “socialist” critique of capitalism acknowledges the climate crisis
and, increasingly, so do some more conservative observers. John Mac Ghlionn, a
conservative writer, posed a radical critique of Trump’s policies in [ _The
Hill_](https://thehill.com/opinion/white-house/5668693-america-decline-trump-
exposed/). He wrote that during Trump’s first term, “he vowed to ‘drain the
swamp,’ revive American industry, tame debt, rebuild trust, and restore
pride.” He adds, “The second time, he [Trump] returned with a sharper edge and
a louder voice, insisting that only he could finish the job he claimed had
been sabotaged the first time around.”

Mac Ghlionn acknowledges the deeper truth of Trump’s presidency: “He was the
messenger. The problem is that America no longer has the political, economic
or cultural capacity to deliver restoration at all.” And he adds: “You can’t
restore a mid-century industrial base in a post-industrial economy with a
single leader. You can’t rebuild trust through [permanent
outrage](https://thehill.com/opinion/white-house/5657224-trump-grocery-prices-
rising/). You can’t borrow your way back to greatness.”

Going further, Mac Ghlionn warns the U.S. “is settling into managed decline.
Each generation inherits a narrower set of possibilities. Boomers dreamed big.
Gen X sought security. Millennials adjusted to constraint. Gen Z dreams of
[not becoming homeless](https://www.multifamilyexecutive.com/property-
management/demographics/report-younger-generations-face-tough-trade-offs-to-
afford-rent).”

Today’s growing socialist movement acknowledges this decline. It does not
identify with Russia, let alone China or the old Soviet Communism, as 21st
century American socialism. However, many don’t share a clear alternative
conception of what socialism means. Rather, it’s a philosophy as well as a
movement in formation.

So far, the U.S.’s socialism 2.0 is a bottom-up popular movement, not a top-
down party system. While sharing many of the same values – e.g.,
affordability, climate change, end foreign wars – individual socialist-
identified candidates (as suggested by the outcome of the 2026 primaries) as
well as local grass-roots activities offer differing analyses. These
differences add voice and vitality of a growing movement.
